title: NGC 2392
caption: The planetary nebula NGC 2392, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
credit: NASA, ESA, Andrew Fruchter (STScI), and the ERO team (STScI + ST-ECF)

recognition.text: Official ESA/Hubble press-release image. No published audience rating.

story: This is NGC 2392, a planetary nebula in the constellation Gemini, made of the glowing remains of a dying star much like the Sun. It was among the first views Hubble captured after the successful servicing mission of December 1999.

A planetary nebula forms when a Sun-like star reaches the end of its life. The star puffs off its outer layers of gas, which drift out into space. The exposed hot core left behind shines with strong ultraviolet light, and that light makes the surrounding gas glow. The name comes from early astronomers, who thought such round fuzzy objects looked a little like planets, but they have nothing to do with planets.

Servicing missions sent astronauts to repair and upgrade Hubble in orbit, and this image came from the telescope's first look at the sky after the one in December 1999. It used filters that pick out the glow of helium, oxygen, hydrogen and nitrogen.

understand.summary: Hubble's Wide Field Planetary Camera 2 imaged the nebula through filters for helium, oxygen, hydrogen-alpha and nitrogen emission. The color mapping isn't published.
understand.eye: Filters that isolate individual gases give each one a color, which is not how an eye would see the nebula.
